title: The Thousand Years and the Great White Throne
summary: An angel binds Satan and seals him in the Abyss for a thousand years, while the martyrs and the faithful come to life and reign with Christ. When the thousand years end, Satan is released, gathers the nations of Gog and Magog against the camp of the saints, and is destroyed by fire and thrown into the lake of fire. Then the dead, great and small, stand before a great white throne and are judged according to their deeds, and Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire.
story: Chapter 19 dealt with the beast and the false prophet. Now the last and oldest enemy, the dragon of chapter 12, “that ancient serpent who is the devil and Satan” (verse 2), meets his end. The words ancient serpent reach all the way back to Genesis 3. The chapter moves from Satan's binding to his release and final defeat, and then to the last judgment of all humanity, clearing the way for the new creation in chapter 21. Whatever one concludes about the thousand years, the chapter's direction is clear: evil is limited, then finished; the dead are raised; everyone is judged; and death itself dies.
historical:
The thousand years (the millennium, from the Latin mille, thousand, and annus, year) is the only place in the Bible that names such a period, and it has been read in several ways since the early church. Some second-century Christian writers, including Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, expected a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth after his return. Augustine, writing The City of God in the early fifth century, argued instead that the thousand years is the present age of the church, and his reading became dominant in the medieval church and among the Protestant Reformers. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries many Puritans and later evangelicals, Jonathan Edwards among them, expected the gospel to spread until a golden age of Christian influence before Christ's return. In the nineteenth century John Nelson Darby developed dispensationalism, spread widely in America by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), which returned to a future earthly millennium within a larger scheme distinguishing God's plans for Israel and the church.

For John's first readers the chapter's setting was persecution. Beheading with a sword or axe (verse 4) was a Roman method of execution, used for Roman citizens among others; by tradition the apostle Paul died this way. Those who had refused to worship the beast or take its mark had lost their lives or their livelihoods, and the vision tells them that the verdict of Roman courts is not the last one.
cultural:
Jewish writers before and around John's time already speculated about a temporary messianic kingdom before the final age. Some texts gave it a set length, though the numbers differed, which shows that a period like this was a familiar idea to John's readers. The names Gog and Magog come from Ezekiel 38-39, where Gog of the land of Magog leads a vast army against God's restored people and is destroyed by God. In Revelation they are no longer a specific northern king and his land but the nations from the four corners of the earth, a picture of all humanity gathered in rebellion.

The books opened at the judgment reflect the ancient practice of written records: kings kept registers and chronicles, and cities kept rolls of citizens. The Old Testament speaks of God's book in this way (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1). Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead, used in the Greek Old Testament to translate Sheol. The sea giving up its dead (verse 13) makes the point that no one is beyond God's reach, not even those lost at sea without a grave, which in the ancient world was counted a special misfortune. The lake of fire and sulfur draws on the fate of Sodom (Genesis 19:24) and on Isaiah's images of burning judgment.
literary: The chapter is made of three visions, each introduced by John's words then I saw: Satan bound (verses 1-3), the thrones and the reign with Christ (verses 4-6), and the great white throne (verses 11-15). Between them comes the account of Satan's release and final defeat (verses 7-10). The phrase a thousand years occurs six times, which shows how much weight it carries, and verse 6 contains the book's fifth beatitude. The battle of verses 7-9 closely resembles the battle of 19:17-21, since both draw on Ezekiel 39, and that similarity is central to the debate over whether chapter 20 follows chapter 19 in time or goes back and retells the same conflict from a new angle. Revelation elsewhere repeats events from different viewpoints, which interpreters call recapitulation, and readers disagree about whether that is happening here.

outline.t: Satan bound and sealed in the Abyss
The faithful reign with Christ: the first resurrection
Satan released, Gog and Magog, and the devil's final defeat
The great white throne and the judgment of the dead

doctrines.note: Every person, great and small, will stand before God and be judged according to their deeds, and those whose names are not in the Book of Life face the second death. The church confesses a final judgment as part of its creed: Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead.

The dead will be raised. The sea, Death, and Hades must give up their dead, and then death itself is destroyed. The bodily resurrection of the dead is the confession of the whole church, however the thousand years are read.
Satan is bound by a single angel with a chain, released only for a brief period, and destroyed by fire from heaven without a battle. The chapter leaves no doubt about who holds power.

Judgment is by deeds, recorded in the books, but the decisive question is whether a name is written in the Book of Life, which 21:27 calls the Lamb's. Deeds reveal a life; the Lamb's book is where rescue comes from.

words.note: Chilioi, a thousand. It appears six times in verses 2-7. Revelation often uses numbers symbolically (seven for completeness, twelve for God's people), and a thousand can mean a vast or complete span, as in Psalm 90:4 and 2 Peter 3:8. Premillennial readers generally take it as a literal period or at least a real future era on earth; amillennial and postmillennial readers generally take it as a symbol for a long, complete age.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. It is the normal New Testament word for the raising of the dead, including Christ's. Verse 5 calls the coming to life of the faithful “the first resurrection.” Premillennial readers take it as a bodily resurrection before the millennium; many amillennial readers take it as the new birth or the believer's life with Christ after death, with the bodily resurrection coming at the end.

Deo, to bind or tie up. Jesus used the same verb when he said no one can plunder a strong man's house without first binding the strong man (Mark 3:27). Amillennial and postmillennial readers connect that saying with this chapter: Satan was bound at Christ's first coming so that he cannot stop the gospel reaching the nations. Premillennial readers see a more complete binding still to come.

Limne, lake. The lake of fire (verses 10, 14, 15) is the final destination of the devil, the beast, the false prophet, Death and Hades, and those not written in the Book of Life. Verse 14 names it “the second death,” meaning final and irreversible separation from God and his life.

christ: The faithful reign “with Christ” (verse 4) and are “priests of God and of Christ” (verse 6), which fulfills the promise of 1:6 and 5:10 and the calling given to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:6). The binding of the strong man points back to Jesus' ministry, where he cast out demons as a sign that the kingdom had come (Matthew 12:28-29). The resurrection in this chapter rests on his, since Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). And the One on the great white throne is, in the New Testament's own teaching, the Son to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22). The chapter's end fulfills Paul's promise that “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:26).

hard.q: What is the thousand years, and when does it happen?
hard.a:
Christians who share the same creed read this chapter in several ways, and it is a second-order question on which faithful believers differ. Historic premillennialism holds that Christ will return before (pre-) the millennium, raise the faithful, and reign on the earth for a long period, after which comes the final rebellion and judgment; it points to the order of chapters 19 and 20 and to two resurrections in verses 4-5, and it has roots in second-century writers. Dispensational premillennialism shares that order but places it within a scheme that keeps distinct promises for Israel and the church, usually with the church taken up to Christ before a seven-year tribulation, and a millennium in which promises to national Israel are fulfilled. Amillennialism (no literal millennium) reads the thousand years as the present age between Christ's first and second comings: Satan is bound so that the nations can hear the gospel, and the faithful who have died reign with Christ now; it notes the symbolic numbers throughout Revelation and reads chapter 20 as a retelling of the same conflict. Postmillennialism holds that Christ returns after (post-) a long era in which the gospel's spread brings great blessing to the world.

Each view has real strengths and faces real questions. Premillennialists must explain why the rest of the New Testament seems to speak of one resurrection and judgment at Christ's return (John 5:28-29); amillennialists must explain the two uses of came to life in verses 4 and 5; postmillennialists must reckon with the book's picture of ongoing persecution until the end. Beneath the differences lies what all of them confess together, which is the first-order faith: Christ will return in glory, the dead will be raised bodily, all will be judged, and death will be destroyed.

questions: The chapter tells persecuted believers that the verdict of human courts is not the final one. Where might that change how you see an unjust situation?
Everyone is judged according to their deeds, yet the Book of Life decides the outcome. How do you hold those two truths together?
Christians have disagreed about the millennium for nearly two thousand years. What does it look like to hold a view with conviction and still treat those who differ as brothers and sisters?
